  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. If the bill misses that window, he said the most likely remaining path is a post-election lame-duck session, and even that depends on Republicans retaining the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune prioritizing the measure over government funding deadlines. He also said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed version is unlikely to advance in the next Congress beginning in January. The article adds that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would likely benefit because major institutions would gain enough confidence to invest in the sector thanks to clearer rules. Cipolaro said the bill would also provide regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing what he called the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class. But he also warned the bill could still fail because negotiations could stall over ethics or decentralized finance enforcement language, or because scheduling delays could prevent action. CoinDesk’s RSS item for the same news cycle, titled “The Clarity Act took a step forward: State of Crypto,” described the issue as unpacking Thursday’s at-times contentious markup hearing. Taken together, the two sources show a single dominant story: Congress advanced the crypto market-structure bill, but the path to law remains narrow, politically fragile, and highly sensitive to the Senate calendar. The shared theme is not just that the bill moved forward, but that the next several weeks may determine whether crypto regulation gets a breakthrough in 2026 or slips into a later political window. The market implication is important because the bill could give Bitcoin clearer treatment under federal law, while also opening the door to broader institutional participation if lawmakers can resolve the remaining disputes. The tone across both sources is cautious: progress is real, but the deadline pressure is increasing. Cointelegraph also noted that the industry is still operating under permanent jurisdictional ambiguity if the legislation stalls, which helps explain why the story matters beyond Washington. The bill is being watched as a signal for whether lawmakers can create a workable framework for the digital asset market, especially at a moment when both policy and market structure debates are moving quickly. The recurring facts across the feeds are the markup passage, the need for 60 votes, the seven-Democrat hurdle, the June-to-early-August window, the midterm risk, and the potential Bitcoin commodity classification. Those are the core details that define the event.",

Cipolaro said Congress has a recess from late July to early September and will then return to a period ahead of the midterm elections in November, when Senate leadership “is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight.”

“If the bill misses that window, the highest-probability remaining pathway becomes a post-election lame-duck session, available only if Republicans hold the Senate and Majority Leader [John] Thune prioritizes it over government funding deadlines,” he added.

Current polling and predictions show a tight race for control of the Senate, with some forecasts showing Republicans with a slight edge, while others put key seats as tossups that could put Democrats in control of the chamber.

Cipolaro said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed crypto market structure bill is unlikely to advance in the next Congress when it begins in January.

“Congressional negotiators face a tradeoff between accepting an imperfect bipartisan framework in 2026 versus risking a substantially different legislative environment after the midterms.”

Cipolaro said that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would get a boost as major institutions would be confident enough to invest in the space because of the legal clarity.

It would also grant regulatory certainty to Bitcoin, classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing “the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class,” he added.

However, Cipolaro said the bill could fail because of stalled negotiations over provisions regarding ethics or decentralized finance enforcement, or because of scheduling delays, which would mean the crypto industry would continue to operate under “permanent jurisdictional ambiguity.”

The US Senate’s crypto market structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms, said Greg Cipolaro, head of research at financial services firm NYDIG.
Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, said earlier this month that he was targeting July 4 for the Senate’s crypto bill to pass, saying there was enough time for a Senate markup, floor vote and House vote. 
“This may represent an aspirational benchmark rather than a fixed legislative deadline,” Cipolaro said in a [note](https://viewemail.nydig.com/crypto-legislation-moves-one-step-forward) on Friday. “The realistic window, however, is June through early August.”
The crypto market structure bill would outline how US watchdogs would regulate crypto and is seen as one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year. However, it has been marred by delays as lawmakers and lobbyists have sought to add or amend provisions around stablecoins and government officials’ use of crypto, among other issues.
The bill [passed a long-delayed markup](https://cointelegraph.com/news/us-senate-banking-committee-advance-clarity-act) in the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday, which voted largely along party lines to advance it to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate and pass.
Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, pictured at the markup. Source: [US Senate](https://www.banking.senate.gov/hearings/05/08/2026/executive-session)
Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority and [will need at least seven Democrats](https://cointelegraph.com/features/crypto-clarity-act-faces-partisan-fight-ethics-senate-floor) on board to pass the bill quickly, but some Democrats are concerned that the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion.
Cipolaro said Congress has a recess from late July to early September and will then return to a period ahead of the midterm elections in November, when Senate leadership “is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight.”
“If the bill misses that window, the highest-probability remaining pathway becomes a post-election lame-duck session, available only if Republicans hold the Senate and Majority Leader [John] Thune prioritizes it over government funding deadlines,” he added.
Current polling and [predictions](https://www.270towin.com/2026-senate-election/consensus-2026-senate-forecast) show a tight race for control of the Senate, with some forecasts showing Republicans with a slight edge, while others put key seats as tossups that could put Democrats in control of the chamber.
Cipolaro said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed crypto market structure bill is unlikely to advance in the next Congress when it begins in January.
“Congressional negotiators face a tradeoff between accepting an imperfect bipartisan framework in 2026 versus risking a substantially different legislative environment after the midterms.”Cipolaro said that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would get a boost as major institutions would be confident enough to invest in the space because of the legal clarity. 
It would also grant regulatory certainty to Bitcoin, classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing “the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class,” he added.
However, Cipolaro said the bill could fail because of stalled negotiations over provisions regarding ethics or decentralized finance enforcement, or because of scheduling delays, which would mean the crypto industry would continue to operate under “permanent jurisdictional ambiguity.”

{
  "topic_theme": "U.S. Senate Crypto Market Structure Bill Faces August Deadline Risk",
  "primary_keyword": "senate crypto bill",
  "primary_headline": "Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG",
  "sources_used": [
    "CoinTelegraph",
    "CoinDesk"
  ],
  "source_urls": [
    "https://cointelegraph.com/news/senate-crypto-bill-august-advance-in-lame-duck-session-nydig?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound",
    "https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/05/17/the-clarity-act-took-a-step-forward-state-of-crypto"
  ],
  "combined_key_facts": [
    "Cointelegraph says the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass, and that it risks not advancing at all if lawmakers miss the window before the midterms.",
    "NYDIG’s Greg Cipolaro says the realistic window is June through early August, after which the highest-probability path becomes a post-election lame-duck session if Republicans keep the Senate.",
    "The article says Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority and would need at least seven Democrats to reach the 60 votes needed to avoid prolonged debate and pass the bill.",
    "CoinDesk’s RSS item frames the same event as the Clarity Act taking a step forward after a contentious markup hearing, showing the bill is advancing but still faces major political friction.",
    "Cipolaro says a signed bill would give markets a boost and bring regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission."
  ],
  "aggregated_raw_content": "Cointelegraph reported under the headline “Senate Crypto Bill Might Pass as Late as August: NYDIG” that the US Senate’s crypto market-structure bill could take until August to pass and risks not advancing at all if lawmakers cannot pass it before the midterms. Greg Cipolaro, head of research at NYDIG, said the July 4 target mentioned earlier by Patrick Witt, a senior White House crypto adviser, looked more like an aspirational benchmark than a fixed legislative deadline. Cipolaro said the realistic window was June through early August. The article explains that the bill is one of the most important pieces of crypto legislation this year because it would outline how US watchdogs regulate crypto, but it has been delayed by disputes over stablecoins, ethics, government officials’ use of crypto, and decentralized finance enforcement. It notes that the Senate Banking Committee passed a long-delayed markup on Thursday and moved the bill to the Senate floor, where it will need 60 votes to avoid prolonged debate. Republicans hold a 53-seat Senate majority, so the bill would need support from at least seven Democrats. Some Democrats argue the bill does not go far enough in preventing crime and sanctions evasion. Cipolaro warned that Congress then faces a narrowing calendar: a recess from late July to early September, then a period leading into the November midterm elections when Senate leadership is unlikely to schedule a contested 60-vote floor fight. If the bill misses that window, he said the most likely remaining path is a post-election lame-duck session, and even that depends on Republicans retaining the Senate and Majority Leader John Thune prioritizing the measure over government funding deadlines. He also said that if Democrats gain control of the Senate, the current Republican-backed version is unlikely to advance in the next Congress beginning in January. The article adds that if the bill is passed and signed into law, crypto markets would likely benefit because major institutions would gain enough confidence to invest in the sector thanks to clearer rules. Cipolaro said the bill would also provide regulatory certainty to Bitcoin by classifying it as a commodity under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and closing what he called the last significant regulatory overhang for Bitcoin as an institutional asset class. But he also warned the bill could still fail because negotiations could stall over ethics or decentralized finance enforcement language, or because scheduling delays could prevent action. CoinDesk’s RSS item for the same news cycle, titled “The Clarity Act took a step forward: State of Crypto,” described the issue as unpacking Thursday’s at-times contentious markup hearing. That framing matches Cointelegraph’s account of the Senate Banking Committee advancing the bill, but it emphasizes that the legislative move was only a step forward rather than final passage. Taken together, the two sources show a single dominant story: Congress advanced the crypto market-structure bill, but the path to law remains narrow, politically fragile, and highly sensitive to the Senate calendar. The shared theme is not just that the bill moved forward, but that the next several weeks may determine whether crypto regulation gets a breakthrough in 2026 or slips into a later political window. The market implication is important because the bill could give Bitcoin clearer treatment under federal law, while also opening the door to broader institutional participation if lawmakers can resolve the remaining disputes. The tone across both sources is cautious: progress is real, but the deadline pressure is increasing. Cointelegraph also noted that the industry is still operating under permanent jurisdictional ambiguity if the legislation stalls, which helps explain why the story matters beyond Washington. The bill is being watched as a signal for whether lawmakers can create a workable framework for the digital asset market, especially at a moment when both policy and market structure debates are moving quickly. The recurring facts across the feeds are the markup passage, the need for 60 votes, the seven-Democrat hurdle, the June-to-early-August window, the midterm risk, and the potential Bitcoin commodity classification. Those are the core details that define the event.",
  "CHART_COIN": "bitcoin"
}
